options.text: It's the right thing to do for the planet
options.feedback: True, and on its own it loses budget decisions. Use it to frame the case, never as the argument.

options.text: Our competitors are already doing it
options.feedback: Weak on its own. The obvious reply is 'and are they seeing a return?'

options.text: Staff have said they'd feel better about working here
options.feedback: Real but unquantified. It supports a case; it can't carry one.

before.feedback: In a budget meeting, sustainability arguments have to be translated into the language of cost, revenue or risk. The ethical case opens the conversation; the financial case closes it.

after.brief: Same skill: which vocabulary is precise enough for a written business case?
after.prompt: Select every term that carries a specific, checkable meaning.

options.text: carbon footprint
options.feedback: Specific and measurable: total emissions attributable to an activity.

options.text: payback period
options.feedback: Precise financial term: the time for savings to cover the initial cost.

options.text: energy consumption
options.feedback: Directly measurable in kWh.

options.text: waste reduction
options.feedback: Measurable against a baseline.

options.text: eco-friendly
options.feedback: Vague marketing language with no agreed definition. Avoid it in a business case.

options.text: green
options.feedback: Too loose to mean anything specific in a written case.

options.text: sustainable
options.feedback: Useful as a heading, but on its own it commits to nothing measurable.

after.feedback: The test for a business case is whether someone could check the claim in twelve months. 'Carbon footprint' passes; 'eco-friendly' does not.

before.brief: A planning meeting. Sort the sentences by future form.
before.prompt: Put each sentence into the right group.

items.text: I'm meeting the client on Tuesday.
We're having lunch with the team on Friday.
We're going to hire two new people.
She's going to start a new project in May.
OK, I'll call him now.
The printer is broken? I'll use the other one.

before.feedback: Things in your calendar: present continuous. Plans you made before: 'going to'. Decisions you make now: 'will'.

after.brief: Same skill, in a chat with a colleague.

items.text: I'm going to visit the Madrid office next month.
We're going to change the website in June.
Tom is going to lead the new project.
It's cold in here. I'll close the window.
You're busy? No problem, I'll do it.
There's no coffee? I'll buy some.

after.feedback: Use 'going to' for plans you made before. Use 'will' when you decide at the moment of speaking.

before.brief: In a job interview, you talk about your last project. Only one version is correct.
before.prompt: Which version is right?

options.text: Last year I worked on our new website. We finished it in May.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Last year' and 'in May' are finished times, so use the past simple: 'worked', 'finished'.

options.text: Last year I have worked on our new website. We have finished it in May.
options.feedback: With 'last year' and 'in May', don't use 'have worked'. Use the past simple.

options.text: Last year I work on our new website. We finish it in May.
options.feedback: This is the present. The project is finished, so add -ed: 'worked', 'finished'.

options.text: Last year I was work on our new website. We was finish it in May.
options.feedback: Don't add 'was' before the verb. Say 'I worked', 'we finished'.

after.brief: Next question: 'What are you doing in your job at the moment?' Only one answer is correct.

options.text: At the moment I'm working on a new app. I usually design the screens.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I'm working' is for now, and 'I usually design' is for your normal job.

options.text: At the moment I work on a new app. I'm usually designing the screens.
options.feedback: The tenses are the wrong way round. Now: 'I'm working'. Usually: 'I design'.

options.text: At the moment I worked on a new app. I usually designed the screens.
options.feedback: 'Worked' is the past. 'At the moment' means now.

options.text: At the moment I'm work on a new app. I usually designing the screens.
options.feedback: Add -ing after 'I'm': 'I'm working'. After 'usually', use 'I design'.

before.brief: A colleague messages you: 'Can you look at the Vidal deck before 2?'  You can, but not until 1:30.
before.prompt: Which reply is best for chat?

options.text: Yes — I'll get to it around 1:30, so you'll have comments before 2. 👍
options.feedback: Answers the question, gives the actual time, and confirms the deadline is safe. Everything they need in one line.

options.text: Yes
options.feedback: Answers but leaves them wondering when, so they may chase you at 1:45.

options.text: I'm quite busy this morning but I should be able to fit it in at some point, I'll try my best to get to it before your deadline if nothing else comes up.
options.feedback: Far too long for chat, and after all those words they still don't know if they'll have it.

options.text: Sure thing!! No problem at all!! 😄😄
options.feedback: Friendly but no time given, and the punctuation is doing a lot of work for a routine request.

after.brief: Different ping: 'Quick one — do we have budget for the extra shoot?' You do not know.

options.text: Not sure — Elena owns that budget line. I'll ask her now and come back to you within the hour.
options.feedback: Says you don't know, names who does, and commits to a time. This is the most useful 'I don't know' you can send.

options.text: I don't know.
options.feedback: True, and it leaves them exactly where they started.

options.text: I think so? Probably fine.
options.feedback: Guessing about money. If it's wrong, someone books a shoot that isn't funded.

options.text: Let me check and I'll let you know.
options.feedback: Helpful. It just doesn't say when, so they don't know whether to wait or chase.

before.brief: You are writing your daily update in the team chat.
before.message: Yesterday I ______ the new login page.
before.prompt: Which word is correct?

options.text: finished
options.feedback: Correct. 'Yesterday' needs the past simple: 'finished'.

options.text: finish
options.feedback: 'Yesterday' is in the past. Use 'finished'.

options.text: am finishing
options.feedback: The present continuous is for now, not for yesterday.

options.text: have finished
options.feedback: Close, but don't use 'have finished' with 'yesterday'.

after.brief: A different chat. Your manager asks where you are today. You reply:
after.message: Sorry, I ______ from home today. My train is cancelled.

options.text: 'm working
options.feedback: Correct. The present continuous is for what is happening now or today.

options.text: worked
options.feedback: That's the past. 'Today' needs 'I'm working'.

options.text: work
options.feedback: The present simple is for habits, like 'I work from home on Fridays'.

options.text: 'm work
options.feedback: Add -ing: 'I'm working'.

before.brief: A customer is angry. His order is two weeks late. Complete what you say.
before.message: I'm very sorry ______ the delay. Let me check your order now.
before.prompt: Which word is correct?

options.text: for
options.feedback: Correct. 'Sorry for' + the problem: 'sorry for the delay'.

options.text: of
options.feedback: Not 'sorry of'. Say 'sorry for the delay'.

options.text: to
options.feedback: 'Sorry to' is followed by a verb: 'sorry to hear that'. Before a noun, use 'for'.

options.text: with
options.feedback: We don't say 'sorry with'. Use 'sorry for'.

after.brief: A different customer waited 20 minutes on the phone. You finish the call.
after.message: Thank you for your ______. Your new order will arrive tomorrow.

options.text: patience
options.feedback: Correct. 'Thank you for your patience' is what we say after a customer waits.

options.text: patient
options.feedback: 'Patient' is an adjective. After 'your', you need the noun: 'patience'.

options.text: delay
options.feedback: 'Thank you for your delay' thanks her for being late! Say 'patience'.

options.text: waiting
options.feedback: 'Thank you for waiting' is correct, but not 'thank you for your waiting'. Use 'your patience'.

before.brief: You are starting a short presentation for a client. Put your opening in order.
before.prompt: Put the lines in the best order.
items: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.
My name is Ana, and I work in the design team.
Today I'm going to show you our new logo.
First, I'm going to explain the idea. Then I'll show you three designs.
At the end, you can ask questions.
before.feedback: Hello and thanks, who you are, the topic, the plan, then questions. 'Going to' tells people your plan.

after.brief: Same skill, at the end of a different presentation, for your own team.
after.prompt: Put the lines in the best order.
items: OK, that's the end of my presentation.
The main point is: we're going to open the new shop in June.
I'm going to send you the full plan next week.
Thank you for listening.
Are there any questions?
after.feedback: Say it's the end and repeat the main point. Then give the next step, say thank you, and ask for questions.

before.brief: A colleague asks you a question over coffee.
before.prompt: Do you prefer working at home or in the office? Why?
checklist: I said my opinion clearly (I think… / In my opinion…)
I gave at least one reason with 'because'
I gave a small example from my work
I spoke for about 30 seconds
before.model: In my opinion, working in the office is better for me. I think it's easier to ask questions, because my colleagues are next to me. For example, last week I had a problem with a report, and my manager helped me in five minutes. But I like working at home on Fridays, because it's quiet.
before.feedback: Opinion, reason, example. This simple plan works for almost any question.

after.brief: A different question, in a team meeting.
after.prompt: What is the best day of the week for team meetings? Why?
checklist: I gave a clear answer (I think… / In my opinion…)
I gave a reason with 'because'
I said one problem with a different day
I finished with a short summary (So, I think…)
after.model: I think Tuesday is the best day for team meetings. On Monday, everyone is busy with emails from the weekend. On Friday, some people work from home. Tuesday is good because we have time to plan the week. So, I think Tuesday morning is best.
after.feedback: A clear opinion, a reason, and a short summary at the end. That is enough for a strong answer.

before.brief: A job interview. The interviewer asks: 'Tell me about your job.'
before.message: I work in the finance ______. I'm responsible for the invoices.
before.prompt: Which word is correct?

options.text: department
options.feedback: Correct. A department is a part of a company, like Finance or Sales.

options.text: responsible
options.feedback: 'Responsible' is an adjective: 'I'm responsible for…'. It is not a place.

options.text: colleague
options.feedback: A colleague is a person, not a part of a company.

options.text: office
options.feedback: Possible, but 'the finance department' is the usual phrase.

after.brief: Next question: 'Who do you work with?'
after.message: I work with five ______, and my manager is the head of finance.

options.text: colleagues
options.feedback: Correct. Colleagues are the people you work with.

options.text: companions
options.feedback: A false friend. At work, say 'colleagues', not 'companions'.

options.text: clients
options.feedback: Clients buy from your company. They are not in your team.

options.text: bosses
options.feedback: Informal, and you have one manager, not five bosses.

before.brief: Your colleague Marta is sick today. You answer her phone. A client says his name very fast.
before.prompt: What do you say?

options.text: Sorry, could you spell your name, please?
options.feedback: Good. Now you can write the name correctly.

options.text: What is your name? Say it again.
options.feedback: Clear, but it sounds like an order. Add 'sorry' and 'could you'.

options.text: OK, thank you.
options.feedback: You didn't understand the name. Now you can't help him.

options.text: Can you spell me your name?
options.feedback: Say 'Could you spell your name, please?' Don't put 'me' after 'spell'.

after.brief: A different call. Marta's manager asks you to do something. There are two files: the price list and the contract.
after.message: Can you send the file to the client today?
after.prompt: You don't know which file. What do you say?

options.text: Sure. Do you mean the price list or the contract?
options.feedback: Good. Two choices make the question quick to answer.

options.text: Which file? I don't understand.
options.feedback: OK, but give two choices. It's faster.

options.text: Sure, no problem.
options.feedback: You don't know which file. You may send the wrong one.

options.text: Can you explain me which file?
options.feedback: Say 'explain to me', or just ask 'Which file do you mean?'

before.brief: You need the meeting link from a colleague. You write in the team chat.
before.prompt: Which message is best for chat?

options.text: Hi Sam, could you send me the link for the 3 p.m. meeting, please?
options.feedback: Friendly, polite and clear. Perfect for chat.

options.text: Link.
options.feedback: Too short. It sounds like an order.

options.text: Dear Mr Jones, I would be very grateful if you could kindly send me the link.
options.feedback: Much too formal for a chat with a colleague.

options.text: Hi Sam, are you there?
options.feedback: Friendly, but it doesn't say what you need. Sam has to ask.

after.brief: A different request. You write to the IT team. You don't know them.

options.text: Hello, my laptop doesn't start. Could you help me today, please? Thanks, Ana (Sales)
options.feedback: Polite and clear. It says the problem, when, and who you are.

options.text: Laptop broken. Fix it.
options.feedback: This is an order, and it is rude.

options.text: Hey guys!! Help!!! 😱
options.feedback: Too informal, and it doesn't say the problem.

options.text: Hello, can you help me?
options.feedback: Polite, but what is the problem? IT needs details.

before.brief: The office manager sent this memo to all staff.
before.prompt: Read the memo and answer the questions.

doc.title: Office closed for the public holiday
doc.text:
The office is closed on Monday 12 May for the public holiday. It opens again on Tuesday 13 May at 8 a.m.

Please send your timesheets by Friday 9 May.

On Saturday 10 May, the IT team is working on the network, so you can't use the shared drive from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. After 5 p.m. it works again.

If you have a question, please call Rosa on extension 214 before Friday.

questions.q: When is the office closed?

options.text: On Monday 12 May
options.feedback: Correct. 'The office is closed on Monday 12 May.'

options.text: On Tuesday 13 May
options.feedback: No. The office opens again on Tuesday.

options.text: On Saturday 10 May
options.feedback: On Saturday the shared drive stops for some hours. The memo does not say the office is closed.

questions.q: What is the deadline for timesheets?

doc.title: Customer survey results — spring
doc.text:
In March we asked 412 customers about their experience with our online shop. Overall, satisfaction has improved: 78% said they were satisfied or very satisfied, compared with 71% last autumn.

The biggest improvement was in delivery. Since we moved to a new courier in January, complaints about late parcels have fallen by half. Customers also liked the new tracking emails.

We recommend introducing QR-code returns, which do not need a printer, before the summer sales.

doc.title: Q2 sales report — Iberia region
doc.text:
Overview: Total revenue for the Iberia region reached €4.2m in Q2, up 9% on Q1 and slightly ahead of the €4.1m forecast. Growth was driven almost entirely by online channels, while store sales remained broadly flat.

Online: Online revenue rose sharply in April following the launch of the new mobile app, and continued to climb, though more gradually, through May and June. By the end of the quarter, online accounted for just over a third of total revenue, compared with roughly a quarter a year ago.

Stores: Store revenue held steady at around €2.7m, unchanged on Q1. Footfall fell by 6%, but the average basket value increased, which largely offset the decline. It is too early to say whether the drop in footfall reflects a long-term shift or simply the unusually wet spring.

B2B: Corporate orders dipped in May, when two major accounts postponed purchases, but recovered in June. We would caution against reading too much into a single month.

Outlook: If current trends continue, online could overtake stores in some product categories by the end of next year. However, this projection assumes that app adoption continues at its current rate, which seems optimistic given that the launch promotion ended in June.

doc.title: Customer support: monthly performance — September
doc.text:
Summary: Ticket volume fell for the third consecutive month, to 3,150 in September, roughly 20% below the June peak. Average first-response time improved from 9 hours to just under 5, the best figure since we started measuring it.

What changed: The drop in volume coincides with the new help centre, which went live in July. Searches on the help centre have tripled, and the proportion of customers who open a ticket after searching has fallen from one in four to one in seven. While this suggests that the help centre is answering questions that would previously have become tickets, we have not yet confirmed this through customer research.

Concerns: Satisfaction with resolved tickets dropped slightly, from 88% to 85%. Comments suggest that some agents may be closing tickets too quickly in order to meet the new response targets. We are reviewing whether the targets are encouraging the wrong behaviour.

Staffing: Two agents left in August and have not been replaced. The team has absorbed their workload so far, but this is unlikely to be sustainable during the November sales period, when volume typically rises by 40–50%.

Recommendation: We recommend approving one temporary hire for November and December, and revisiting the response targets before the end of the year.

doc.title: Annual client survey — key findings
doc.text:
This year's survey was completed by 186 of our 450 corporate clients, a response rate of 41%. This is higher than last year, but it still means that most clients did not take part, so the findings should be read with some caution.

Overall satisfaction remained high, with 82% of respondents rating our service as good or excellent. Account management was once again the most praised area; several clients mentioned their account manager by name, which suggests that personal relationships remain a key strength.

Pricing was the area with the lowest scores. However, the comments were not uniformly negative: a number of clients said our prices were higher than competitors' but justified by the quality of the work. Smaller clients were noticeably more critical than larger ones, particularly about the cost of revisions.

The new online portal received mixed feedback. Clients who had used it rated it well, but nearly half of respondents said they were not aware it existed, which points to a communication problem rather than a product problem.

We propose three actions: a targeted campaign to promote the portal, a review of pricing for clients spending under €20,000 a year, and follow-up interviews with the ten clients who gave the lowest scores.

before.brief: A publisher is making story cards for a children's book. The cards for 'The Tortoise and the Hare' are mixed up.
before.prompt: Put the parts of the story in the right order.
items: A fast hare laughs at a slow tortoise, and the tortoise says: 'Let's have a race.'
The race starts. The hare runs far ahead and decides to sleep under a tree.
The tortoise walks slowly but never stops, and passes the sleeping hare.
The hare wakes up and runs, but it's too late: the tortoise wins.
The lesson: slow and steady wins the race.

items: Lisbon, 1998. Inês is twenty-three and works in her grandfather's small restaurant.
One day, a letter arrives: the building is sold, and the restaurant must close in three months.
Inês decides to enter a famous cooking competition. The prize is enough to save the restaurant.
On the night of the final, her grandfather falls ill, and she has to cook alone.
In the end, she doesn't win, but a food critic in the audience changes everything.
after.feedback: Setting and character first, then the problem (the conflict), then the plan, the climax (the final night) and the ending (the resolution).

before.feedback: 'Like' or 'as' → simile. One thing IS another → metaphor. A thing breathes, whispers or watches → personification.

after.feedback: Hyperbole makes things bigger; understatement makes them smaller (often for humour); an oxymoron puts two opposite words together.

before.brief: You're writing to an author with notes on the first chapter of her novel. Choose the right term for each gap.
before.prompt: Complete the email.
before.text:
Dear Helen,

Thank you for chapter one. We love the opening line, 'The city was a sleeping animal'. It's a powerful {}, and it sets the mood immediately.

On page 3, 'the wind whispered through the trees' is a nice piece of {}, but we have the wind whispering again on page 5. Could you change one of them?

We also liked 'as quiet as snow'. This {} is simple and clear. Finally, 'I've told you a million times' is obviously {}, so it works well in Sam's dialogue: it sounds like real speech.

Best wishes,
Marta

gaps.feedback: No 'like' or 'as': the city IS an animal. That's a metaphor.
The wind does something human, whispering: personification.
'As quiet as' compares with 'as': a simile.
Nobody has said it a million times: it's a deliberate exaggeration, hyperbole.

after.brief: The translator of the novel has questions. You reply with the editor's explanations.
after.text:
Hi Pierre,

Thanks for your questions. 'A deafening silence' is an {}: two opposite ideas side by side, so please keep both words in French.

When Sam says 'It's just a scratch' about his broken arm, that's {}. He makes it sound small, which shows he's brave, or proud.

In chapter 4, the fire station burns down. This is {}: the opposite of what we expect. And the red scarf that appears in every chapter is a {}: it stands for Helen's lost sister.

Best,
Marta

gaps.feedback: Two contradictory words together, 'deafening' and 'silence': an oxymoron.
Making something serious sound small is understatement, the opposite of hyperbole.
A gap between what we expect and what happens: situational irony.
An object that stands for a bigger idea is a symbol.

before.brief: You work for a poetry magazine. Next month's feature is on Walt Whitman, and you're checking the notes before they go to print.
before.prompt: Read the poem and answer the questions.

doc.title: A Noiseless Patient Spider
doc.text:
A noiseless patient spider,
I mark'd where on a little promontory it stood isolated,
Mark'd how to explore the vacant, vast surrounding,
It launched forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself,
Ever unreeling them, ever tirelessly speeding them.

And you O my soul where you stand,
Surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space,
Ceaselessly musing, venturing, throwing, seeking the spheres to connect them,
Till the bridge you will need be form'd, till the ductile anchor hold,
Till the gossamer thread you fling catch somewhere, O my soul.

questions.q: How is the poem organised?

options.text: Two stanzas of five lines, in free verse
options.feedback: Correct. Two groups of five lines, with no regular rhyme or metre.

options.text: Fourteen lines with a rhyme scheme: it's a sonnet
options.feedback: It has ten lines and no rhyme scheme.

options.text: Three stanzas with a refrain
options.feedback: There are two stanzas, and no repeated refrain line.

questions.q: Why does the poet repeat 'filament, filament, filament'?

options.text: To imitate the spider sending out thread after thread
options.feedback: Correct. The repetition copies the repeated action.

options.text: Because he has forgotten the word for 'thread'
options.feedback: The repetition is deliberate: it has an effect.

options.text: To make the line rhyme with the next one
options.feedback: The poem doesn't rhyme. The repetition imitates the spinning.

questions.q: Which phrase uses alliteration?

options.text: 'vacant, vast'
options.feedback: Correct. The 'v' sound repeats at the start of both words.

options.text: 'out of itself'
options.feedback: The words don't begin with the same consonant sound.

options.text: 'where you stand'
options.feedback: No repeated first consonant here.

questions.q: What does the second stanza compare to the spider?

options.text: The speaker's soul
options.feedback: Correct. 'And you O my soul…': the soul is also alone, reaching out to connect.

options.text: The ocean
options.feedback: 'Oceans of space' describe where the soul is, but it's the soul that is compared to the spider.

options.text: A bridge
options.feedback: The bridge is what the soul hopes to build.

after.brief: Now the magazine's 'Classic of the month' page. A reader has written in with questions about this sonnet.
after.prompt: Read the poem and answer the questions.

doc.title: Sonnet 18
doc.text:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date;
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st;
Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

questions.q: How many lines does a sonnet have?

options.text: Fourteen
options.feedback: Correct. Count them: fourteen lines is the mark of a sonnet.

options.text: Ten
options.feedback: Ten is the Whitman poem. A sonnet has fourteen.

options.text: Sixteen
options.feedback: A sonnet has fourteen lines.

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of the first four lines (day / temperate / May / date)?

options.text: ABAB
options.feedback: Correct. 'day' rhymes with 'May' (A), 'temperate' with 'date' (B).

options.text: AABB
options.feedback: 'day' and 'temperate' don't rhyme. The rhymes alternate.

options.text: There is no rhyme: it's free verse
options.feedback: Sonnets have a fixed rhyme scheme. Free verse doesn't.

questions.q: The last two lines end with 'see' and 'thee'. What are they called?

options.text: A rhyming couplet
options.feedback: Correct. Two lines together that rhyme close the poem.

options.text: A stanza of free verse
options.feedback: They rhyme, so they are not free verse.

options.text: Enjambment
options.feedback: Enjambment is when a sentence runs past the end of a line.

questions.q: Which phrase uses alliteration?

options.text: 'every fair from fair'
options.feedback: Correct. The 'f' sound repeats at the start of 'fair', 'from' and 'fair'.

options.text: 'darling buds'
options.feedback: The first sounds are different: 'd' and 'b'.

options.text: 'summer's lease'
options.feedback: The first sounds are different: 's' and 'l'.

the same vowel sound in nearby words: 'go slow over the road'
the pattern of end rhymes, shown with letters: ABAB

a sentence that runs on past the end of a line
poetry without a fixed rhyme scheme or metre

before.brief: You're editing the teacher's guide for a poetry anthology. Four contributors wrote a sentence on the same line from Whitman: 'It launched forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself'.
before.prompt: Which sentence should go into the guide?

options.text: Whitman's epizeuxis ('filament, filament, filament') imitates the spider's repeated spinning, which makes the soul's effort to connect feel patient and endless.
options.feedback: Device, evidence and effect, and it links the image to the poem's larger meaning.

options.text: Whitman repeats the word 'filament' three times in line 4.
options.feedback: Accurate, but only an observation. Why does it matter?

options.text: The repetition of 'filament' is very effective and powerful.
options.feedback: 'Effective' and 'powerful' sound like analysis but say nothing. Effective at doing what?

options.text: Whitman was obviously a lonely man who spent a lot of time watching spiders.
options.feedback: Guesswork about the poet's life, not analysis of the words, and it confuses the poet with the speaker.

after.brief: Now a sentence on Dickinson's 'We talked as Girls do'. The editor wants the strongest one about her dashes, as in 'We – occupy – Degree –'.

options.text: Dickinson's dashes ('We – occupy – Degree –') break the line into hesitant fragments, so the memory seems to return in pieces, and thoughts are left open rather than finished.
options.feedback: It quotes, names the technique, and explains two effects, on rhythm and on meaning.

options.text: Dickinson uses a lot of dashes, which was typical of her style.
options.feedback: True, but it describes her habit rather than what the dashes do in this poem.

options.text: The dashes make the poem more interesting to read.
options.feedback: Too vague. More interesting how?

options.text: The dashes show that Dickinson was nervous when she wrote the poem.
options.feedback: A guess about the writer, not an effect on the reader. Analyse the text, not the author's state of mind.

before.brief: The anthology editor, Dr. Rahman, needs a short note for the teacher's guide on the last lines of Dickinson's poem.
before.message: Could you send me a short paragraph on the ending of 'We talked as Girls do'? The last four lines are: 'We parted with a contract / To cherish, and to write / But Heaven made both, impossible / Before another night.' What device is at work, and what effect does it have? Thanks, Nadia Rahman
before.prompt: Write your email.
before.task: Reply to Dr. Rahman with a short analytical paragraph on the ending: name one or two devices, quote the text, and explain the effect. Write about the speaker, not about Dickinson's life.
include: The effect on meaning or on the reader

checks.label: Writes about the speaker, not the poet's life
Avoids guessing at the poet's feelings

selfCheck: Does every quotation have an effect after it?
Did I avoid retelling the poem line by line?
before.model:
Dear Nadia,

Here is a paragraph for the ending.

The last lines turn the poem on its legal metaphor. The girls part with a 'contract / To cherish, and to write', but 'Heaven made both, impossible / Before another night'. The irony is sharp: the speaker and her friend imagined themselves as 'Disposers' of destiny, yet a higher authority cancels their agreement in a single line. Death is never named, and the flat, almost administrative wording works as understatement, which makes the loss feel colder than open lament. The full rhyme of 'write / night' seals the ending with finality.

Best wishes,
Marta

after.brief: Dr. Rahman liked your note. Now she wants one on the turn in Whitman's poem.
after.message: Lovely, thank you. Could you do the same for 'A Noiseless Patient Spider'? I'm interested in the moment the poem changes: 'And you O my soul where you stand, / Surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space'. Nadia
after.task: Write a short analytical paragraph on the turn at the start of the second stanza: name the devices, quote the text, explain the effect, and suggest how it connects the two stanzas.
include: The apostrophe ('O my soul') or another device named
The effect, and how it links the spider and the soul

checks.label: Connects the spider and the soul

selfCheck: Did I explain why the turn matters, not just where it is?
Is each device followed by its effect?
after.model:
Dear Nadia,

Here's the paragraph on the turn.

The second stanza opens with an apostrophe, 'And you O my soul', and the speaker stops observing the spider and addresses his own soul. This marks the poem's turn from outer description to inner reflection, and it reveals the first stanza as one half of an extended metaphor: the soul, like the spider, stands alone and reaches out. The paradox of 'Surrounded, detached' and the metaphor 'measureless oceans of space' stress both the scale of the universe and the soul's isolation within it, which makes its effort to connect seem all the more fragile and brave.

Best,
Marta

before.brief: You're preparing the pack for a reading group. Before you write the discussion questions, check that you understand the poem.
before.prompt: Read the poem and answer the questions.

doc.title: We talked as Girls do
doc.text:
We talked as Girls do –
Fond, and late –
We speculated fair, on every subject, but the Grave –
Of our's, none affair –
We handled Destinies, as cool –
As we – Disposers – be –
And God, a Quiet Party
to our authority –
But fondest, dwelt upon Ourself
As we eventual – be –
When Girls, to Women, softly raised
We – occupy – Degree –
We parted with a contract
To cherish, and to write
But Heaven made both, impossible
Before another night.

questions.q: Where is the main irony of the poem?

options.text: The girls see themselves as 'Disposers' of destiny, yet Heaven cancels their plans 'Before another night'.
options.feedback: Correct. Confidence in controlling the future against the sudden reality of death: situational irony.

options.text: The girls talk late into the night although they are tired.
options.feedback: That's a detail of the scene, not an irony.

options.text: God is described as 'a Quiet Party'.
options.feedback: That's a bold metaphor, and it sets up the irony, but the irony lies in the outcome.

questions.q: How is death presented?

options.text: It is never named: it is 'the Grave' and 'Heaven'.
options.feedback: Correct. Euphemism and understatement keep death at a distance, which makes it colder.

options.text: It is described in vivid, violent detail.
options.feedback: The opposite: the poem never describes it.

options.text: It is personified as a visitor at the door.
options.feedback: Not in this poem. Heaven acts, but death itself is not a character.

questions.q: How does the tone change?

options.text: From nostalgic and playful to flat and matter-of-fact
options.feedback: Correct. The lively talk gives way to two quiet, final lines.

options.text: From angry to forgiving
options.feedback: There is no anger in the poem.

options.text: It stays cheerful throughout.
options.feedback: The last two lines change everything.

questions.q: Words such as 'Party', 'authority', 'contract' and 'Degree' form…

options.text: an extended legal metaphor
options.feedback: Correct. Friendship is framed as a binding agreement, which a higher authority then cancels.

options.text: a rhyme scheme
options.feedback: These words aren't linked by sound but by meaning: the language of law and business.

options.text: a refrain
options.feedback: A refrain is a repeated line, and none of these is repeated.

after.brief: For the second session, the group is reading a short story. Here's the opening. Check the pack's notes on it.
after.prompt: Read the extract and answer the questions.

doc.title: The Locked Room (opening)
meta: A short story, for the reading group
doc.text:
Every morning, Mrs Hale dusted every room in the house except one. The door at the end of the corridor stayed locked, as it had for eleven years, and the key stayed on the chain around her neck.

When the new lodger arrived, he asked about it on his first evening. 'Storage,' she said. 'Nothing interesting.' He noticed that she touched the key as she said it.

The next week, a letter came from the council: the house would be inspected on Monday, every room. Mrs Hale read it twice, folded it into a small square, and put it in her apron.

On Sunday, the sky turned black and the storm cut the power to the whole street. 'What a wonderful evening,' she said, lighting a candle, and she smiled for the first time since the letter came.

questions.q: The locked door is mentioned several times. What is it?

options.text: A motif, and possibly a symbol of a secret or a past she hides
options.feedback: Correct. It recurs (motif) and suggests something beyond itself (symbol).

options.text: The setting of the story
options.feedback: The house is the setting. The door is a recurring detail inside it.

options.text: An example of onomatopoeia
options.feedback: Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound.

questions.q: Why might 'What a wonderful evening' be ironic?

options.text: A storm and a power cut are not 'wonderful', unless the storm helps her hide something before the inspection.
options.feedback: Correct. The words say the opposite of the situation, which hints at a hidden meaning.

options.text: Because the evening really is beautiful
options.feedback: The sky is black and the power is cut. The gap is the point.

options.text: Because she is lying about the lodger
options.feedback: The irony is in her comment on the storm.

questions.q: What is the mood of the extract?

options.text: Uneasy and suspenseful
options.feedback: Correct. The secret, the letter and the storm build tension.

options.text: Joyful and relaxed
options.feedback: Her smile is unsettling rather than joyful, given everything before it.

options.text: Angry
options.feedback: Nobody shows anger. The atmosphere is tense.

questions.q: Her answer, 'Storage. Nothing interesting', while touching the key, suggests…

options.text: that the reader shouldn't fully trust what she says
